concept.body:
Behind “X% of jobs” sit four different quantities:

| Quantity | Question |
|---|---|
| **Exposure** | Does a technology overlap with tasks of an occupation? |
| **Technical potential** | Could tasks be automated with today's technology? |
| **Forecast** | What does a model expect for future jobs? |
| **Measured effect** | What actually changed after a deployment? |

Frey and Osborne estimated theoretical automation probabilities for US occupations in 2013. The OECD Employment Outlook 2023 reports employment shares in occupations at high risk of automation without forecasting job losses for Germany. The IAB calculates which share of core tasks could technically be substituted and stresses that substitutability does not mean automation happens.

Whether an employer deploys depends on cost, liability, data quality, review effort and co-determination.
concept.takeaway: For every jobs figure, first ask which of the four quantities is being measured.

sources.label: Frey & Osborne (2013): The Future of Employment

exercise.title: Sort eight headlines
exercise.instructions: File each invented headline under the quantity it actually measures. Every placement is explained at once. You are done when all eight are sorted.

items.why: “Touches” means overlap. The figure does not say whether jobs disappear or only workflows change.

items.text: “Language models could affect 40% of lawyers' working time”
items.why: “Affect” describes exposure. Affected time can also mean extra review work.

items.text: “70% of core tasks in manufacturing jobs could technically be substituted today”
items.why: “Could be substituted” is the IAB logic of substitution potential: technically possible, not deployed.

items.text: “Half of all bookkeeping steps could be fully automated with market-ready software”
items.why: Market-ready technology, conditional mood: this measures potential. Cost, data quality and liability decide deployment.

items.text: “One in three jobs will vanish by 2035”
items.why: A statement about future jobs is a forecast. Check whether the source models it or merely relabels exposure.

items.text: “AI will cost millions of jobs by 2030”
items.why: A year plus a job count: a forecast. Without assumptions about adoption, demand and new tasks it cannot be checked.

items.text: “After introducing a chatbot, company X cut 12% of its call-centre jobs”
items.why: An observed change in one company. It holds for that case, not for an industry.

items.text: “Survey: 15% of firms hired fewer people because of AI”
items.why: Self-reported effect that already happened. Check the sample and the question wording.

checks.prompt: A study reports “high exposure for tax clerks”. What follows?

options.text: Many of their tasks overlap with the technology; it says nothing about jobs.
The occupation will disappear in the next few years.
options.feedback: That would be a forecast. Exposure only measures overlap with tasks.

options.text: Employers have already deployed the technology.
options.feedback: Exposure says nothing about actual deployment. That would be a measured effect.

checks.explanation: Exposure is the starting point of an analysis, not a result about jobs.

checks.prompt: What does the IAB stress about substitution potential?

options.text: Technically substitutable does not mean the task will actually be automated.
It is a forecast of job losses up to 2030.
options.feedback: The IAB works with today's market-ready technology and makes no jobs forecast.

options.text: It measures how many firms already use AI.
options.feedback: Use is deployment. Potential describes what would be technically possible.

checks.explanation: Potential is a snapshot of what is technically possible. Deployment and employment depend on further factors.

lessons.title: Your task profile
lessons.subtitle: Assess tasks, not occupations, and measure the benefit yourself

concept.body:
An occupation is a bundle of tasks. Technical potential tends to be high when a step repeats, has digital inputs and follows clear rules, such as transferring data or checking completeness. Automation gets hard with changing physical surroundings, rare exceptions, responsibility for safety and work with people. None of this makes a job “AI-proof”: documentation and planning change in care work and trades too.

Whether AI saves you time is shown by a measurement, not a profile: the same task with and without the tool, including the time spent checking and correcting.

In Germany, if a tool records performance or behaviour, the works council has a co-determination right under Section 87(1) no. 6 BetrVG (Works Constitution Act), unless a statute or collective agreement already settles the matter.
concept.takeaway: Exposure describes tasks. You measure the benefit including review time, not by feel.

exercise.title: Map your working week
exercise.instructions: Spread your weekly hours across three task types and set two assumptions. The calculator shows your exposure profile and the net effect of your assumptions. You are done when both tasks are complete.

inputs.label: Repetitive, digital, rule-based
inputs.help: e.g. transferring data, checking forms, standard texts

inputs.label: Digital, with judgement
inputs.help: e.g. analyses, drafts, advice by e-mail

inputs.label: On site, physical or with people
Assumption: time saved on rule-based steps
Assumption: review effort as a share of the saving

outputs.label: Net hours per week under your assumptions
outputs.help: Only as good as your assumptions. Measuring beats estimating.

verdicts.title: High exposure, not a forecast
verdicts.body: Many steps could technically be automated. Whether your job changes depends on deployment, review effort and new tasks.

verdicts.title: Mixed profile
verdicts.body: Individual steps may change. Test them with approved tools and test data.

verdicts.title: Low exposure, not AI-proof
verdicts.body: Documentation, planning and information search change here too.

goals.label: Map a week of at least 20 hours
goals.insight: That is your exposure profile. It describes tasks, not the future of your job.

goals.label: Set the review effort to “all of it”
goals.insight: Then nothing is left. Only a measurement that includes review time shows whether AI saves time.

props.note: A rough split using the traits from the concept. Not an occupational forecast; you set the assumptions yourself.

checks.prompt: Which task tends to have high technical potential?

options.text: Transferring invoice data from PDFs into a spreadsheet.
Agreeing a care plan with relatives at the bedside.
options.feedback: A changing situation, relationships and responsibility make automation hard.

options.text: Inspecting a building site with unknown ground conditions.
options.feedback: Changing physical surroundings and rare exceptions argue against high potential.

checks.explanation: Repetitive, digital and rule-based: these are the traits of high technical potential.

checks.prompt: Your team wants to know whether an AI tool saves time. What is the most reliable way?

options.text: Measure the same task with and without the tool, including review and correction time.
Take the time saving from the vendor's claim.
options.feedback: Vendor claims come from other workflows and data. You measure your own process.

options.text: Ask after a week how it feels.
options.feedback: Perceived time often underestimates review. A measurement against a baseline is more reliable.

checks.explanation: A controlled comparison against a baseline shows the benefit. Review time is part of it.
